title: Pigs that play video games
hook: In a lab experiment, pigs steered a joystick with their snouts to hit targets.
peek: Researchers taught four pigs to move a cursor on a screen by nudging a joystick with their snouts. The pigs hit targets far more often than chance would allow, though they never quite matched the scores of monkeys on the same kind of task.
lede: In the late 1990s, animal scientist Candace Croney and psychologist Sarah Boysen began an unusual test at Penn State. They gave pigs a joystick, adapted from equipment used with primates, and a computer screen. Nudging the stick with their snouts, the pigs learned to move a cursor into target areas on the screen. When they hit a target, a machine dropped a food treat.

bullets.text: Four pigs took part: two large Yorkshire pigs named Hamlet and Omelette, and two small Panepinto micro pigs named Ebony and Ivory. The results were finally published in 2021 in Frontiers in Psychology.
All four pigs hit the targets well above chance, even as the tasks were made harder. That suggests they understood that their snout movements controlled the cursor.

Pigs are farsighted and the task was built for hands, not snouts, which made their scores more striking. They did not reach the accuracy of monkeys tested on similar tasks, a gap the authors linked partly to these limits.

When the treat dispenser broke down, the pigs kept playing for a while with only encouraging words from the researchers. The team took this as a sign that the social side of the task mattered to them.
